title: Plan My Arts Project And Role
objective: Choose an arts project, plan its purpose and intended outcomes, and define the pupil’s own leadership role within the separate Arts leadership unit.

blocks.text: Silver · Unit 2 · Part 2A · Plan my arts project and role.
Unit 2 is Arts leadership. You will plan an arts project and your own role in leading it. Your Unit 1 work can inform your choice, but the two units keep separate evidence.

Leadership means helping people work towards an arts purpose. It can involve explaining, listening, organising choices and responding when someone needs support. It does not require being the loudest person.
Today you choose a project and a role that you can describe clearly. The practical plan, real delivery, work with others and review follow in later stages of the project.

This deck directly evidences Silver Unit 2 Part 2A, Plan the project and own leadership role. Source of award requirements: tools/artsaward/SPEC.json, Silver and universal rules. Silver is the Level 2 Award in the Arts, with TWO units evidenced separately. Mark parts P / A / N. ONE Attempted allowed PER UNIT. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass. Results are Pass / Below Pass only. The 20-file cap applies across the whole Silver portfolio, not per unit or lesson. Keep both units and all parts separately identifiable. Nine cumulative part files or two unit files with part sections are optional layouts, not award requirements. Every locator names the actual file plus page, slide or timecode. The four assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, planning and review, and communication. Only an adviser trained at Silver may assess. Delivery is through a validated centre; staff must confirm both conditions, which this deck does not assert are met. Advisers must not write plans, reviews or evidence for pupils. Read, prompt or scribe the pupil’s exact words and check them back without improving them. Core, Extend and Challenge vary support within Silver; each retains the full evidence meaning and the pupil’s own choices. Keep adult models and source quotations distinct from the pupil’s evidence. No forced private disclosure, public performance, filming or posting. Fourteen forty-minute lesson spines do not deliver the whole 95-hour programme; record actual additional guided and independent work.

Silver Unit 2 Part 2A requires planning the project and the pupil’s own leadership role. Use actual interests, skills, access needs and available resources to support a genuine pupil choice. Example projects in this deck are optional teaching models, not a set project or a quota for group size, sessions or outcomes. Prepare plain planning paper or use the included focus rows, safe sample materials and information about feasible local resources. Staff should identify possible willing participants and practical limits without promising that anyone has agreed. No venue, event or public showing is asserted or required by this deck. A project may use skills developed in Unit 1, but Unit 2 must have separately identifiable leadership planning, action and review. Do not relabel the pupil’s own practice challenge as a leadership project. Model an adult plan first, explicitly separate from pupil evidence. Staff may prompt and scribe exactly but must not supply the pupil’s project choice or write their role for them.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve

blocks.text: Look at art you have made or a method you have explored. Which skill could you explain clearly, or which art idea could you help a group develop? Use your actual experience to choose a starting point.

Think about the people who might take part. They could be willing peers, a small group or staff learners. What might help them enjoy or understand the art activity? Do not assume they have already agreed.
List an interest you bring and a responsibility you might manage. You can write, speak or use labelled pictures. Your plan should show your own thinking rather than a role chosen for you.

stages.data-ta1: Help the pupil use real work and interests. Record potential people as potential until agreed. Do not allocate a leadership role merely because it is convenient for staffing.

stages.title: Starter · create the need

blocks.text: Compare two project statements. First: We will do some art and I will help. Second: I will lead a print activity so learners can explore repeated shapes. I will demonstrate a print and guide their choices.
The second statement names an arts purpose and a leadership responsibility. We can begin to picture what the leader will do. The first leaves both the art and the help unclear.
A project aim describes what you want the activity to achieve. Your role describes what you personally will lead. A group may share an aim while each person holds a different responsibility.
You do not need to run a large event. A manageable project can give you real decisions to make, people to work with and useful evidence to review later.

stages.data-ta1: Read both examples aloud. Use them to distinguish aim from role rather than imposing the print project. Accept an accessible, small-scale project that still gives the pupil genuine leadership.

stages.title: I Do · model

blocks.text: Watch me plan an example before you make your own choice. My model project is a print activity for a small willing group. I want the learners to explore how a repeated shape can create a pattern.
I consider what I could lead. I could explain the task, model a safe print, ask learners about their choices and help them compare results. These actions connect my role to the arts purpose.
I also name what belongs to others. An adult checks the room and materials. Learners choose their own shapes and spaces. I do not take over their artwork just because I lead the activity.

blocks.title: Connect the project to your role
blocks.caption: Your responsibility should help the arts purpose happen.
blocks.alt: PURPOSE: what the art can achieve. PEOPLE: who may take part. MY ROLE: what I will lead. OUTCOME: what we hope to see. Your responsibility should help the arts purpose happen.

blocks.text: I picture an outcome: learners can show a pattern and explain a choice. I will later plan how to find out whether that happened. At this point it is an intention, not a result.
This example shows how to connect ideas. It is not a plan for you to copy. Your arts purpose, people and responsibility should suit the project you choose.

stages.data-ta1: Use the model as adult teaching material only. Distinguish intended outcome from claimed delivery. Model a meaningful pupil role while retaining necessary adult safety responsibilities.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits

blocks.text: Sort the visible cards into PROJECT AIM, MY LEADERSHIP ROLE, or NEEDS DETAIL. Think about whether the words explain a purpose or a personal action.

items: 1. Help learners explore texture through a shared collage.
2. I will show how to join two papers and invite learners to test the join.
3. My role is to do everything.
4. Give the group a way to choose and arrange work for a small display.
5. I will guide the choice of labels and check that each maker’s view is heard.
6. We will have a good time with some stuff.

blocks.text: The key is PROJECT AIM: 1 and 4; MY LEADERSHIP ROLE: 2 and 5; NEEDS DETAIL: 3 and 6. A useful role names something you can actually do and later review.
Improve one unclear card together. Keep the arts purpose and a manageable responsibility visible. You are practising a planning method before you write your own plan.

stages.data-ta1: Every card and the key are provided. Gather individual choices before discussion. Do not replace the pupil’s later role with the class model answer.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect

blocks.text: A group project can make responsibility hard to see. I separate the team’s shared work from my own decisions so a reader can understand my contribution.

blocks.title: Name the shared project and your part
blocks.caption: A shared outcome still needs an identifiable personal role.
blocks.alt: THE GROUP PROJECT: shared arts purpose, people work together. MY LEADERSHIP: actions I take responsibility for, decisions I can explain. A shared outcome still needs an identifiable personal role.

blocks.text: For my model, the group may arrange a small display. My role could be to guide the choice of labels. I would ask what each maker wants viewers to notice and help agree a clear order.
Someone else could lead the physical layout. I would listen to that person and agree how our tasks connect. Naming my role does not mean I work alone.
I also check whether I know enough to lead the task. If I need to practise the method or ask for access support, I include that as preparation. I do not claim a skill I have not tried.

stages.data-ta1: Use a distinct group-project example to show role boundaries. The shared aim is not enough by itself; preserve each pupil’s own proposed responsibility and any preparation needs.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab

blocks.text: Consider two feasible project ideas. You might lead a print activity, guide a group collage or help a group select and explain work for a display. You may suggest another arts project.
For each idea, name the arts purpose and a role you could lead. Check whether the materials, people and your current skills make it a sensible choice.
Talk with a partner or adult about the trade-off. Which option gives you a clear responsibility and suits the people who may take part? Keep your reasons; the final choice is yours.

stages.data-ta1: Offer actual feasibility information without choosing for the pupil. Use safe sample materials for a small rehearsal if useful. Discussion with a helper supports planning but is not project delivery.

stages.title: Independent · evidence

blocks.text: Choose your arts project and record its purpose. Identify the people who may take part and the outcome you hope to support. State what still needs agreement.
Define your own leadership role through concrete actions. Explain how those actions serve the arts purpose. If you are working in a team, distinguish your role from the responsibilities of others.

items: Core: use prompts, labelled pictures or an exact scribe to record your own chosen arts project and personal leadership role. Include the purpose, intended outcome and any needed preparation.
Extend: make the same pupil-chosen project and role plan in your own format, connecting your responsibilities to the purpose and intended outcome.
Challenge: retain the same project and personal role evidence. Compare a second feasible option and explain why your chosen responsibility offers the best fit.

blocks.text: Keep the first version before you revise it after feedback. Your plan can change as you learn more. The record should show which choices were yours and why you made them.

stages.data-ta1: All support routes retain the pupil’s own project choice and leadership-role plan. Scribe exact words and check them back. Do not write a more polished adult plan in place of the pupil’s account.

stages.title: Exit · check the trail

blocks.text: Explain your plan to a partner or adult. Can they tell what the arts project aims to achieve and what you personally will lead? If either is unclear, make a specific change.
Save the plan under Silver Unit 2 Part 2A. Record the actual file name plus page, slide or timecode. Keep this separate from the Unit 1 arts-challenge record.
Identify one practical issue to investigate next, such as materials or who might take part. Your project is planned at this stage; real delivery and its review still need to happen.

stages.data-ta1: Check actual plan locators and separate Unit 2 labelling. Distinguish proposals from agreed arrangements. Carry practical questions into 2B without presenting the plan as delivered leadership.
